title: Hooks State Machine & Closures
description: Hooks linked-list architecture, rules of hooks validator, stale closures, useInterval, useEffectEvent, and effect phase scheduling.

subtopics.title: Hooks Linked List & Rules of Hooks
subtopics.summary: memoizedState pointer list on fiber, call order stability, why hooks cannot be in if-statements.
subtopics.mentalModel: React stores hook states on the Fiber's `memoizedState` property as a singly linked list (`hook.next`). On every render, React traverses this list in the exact order hooks are called. If a hook call is conditional, the list indices drift, corrupting all subsequent hook states.
subtopics.traps: Calling hooks inside `if (condition)`, loops, or nested functions, causing silent state corruption or invariant crashes.

questions.title: Simulate useState Hook in Pure JS
questions.subtopicTitle: Hooks Linked List & Rules of Hooks
questions.concept: Hook State Holder and Setter Dispatcher
questions.problemStatement: Implement `createSimpleUseState(initialValue)` that returns a pair `[getState, setState]`. Calling `setState(newValueOrFn)` updates state, and `getState()` returns the current value.

testCases.name: Initializes and updates with direct values
testCases.testFn: const [get, set] = createSimpleUseState(0); set(42); return get();

testCases.name: Supports functional updater syntax
testCases.testFn: const [get, set] = createSimpleUseState(10); set(prev => prev + 5); return get();

testCases.name: Supports lazy initial state function

Supports functional updater syntax
Supports lazy initial state function

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: React Hooks do not use magic; they are implemented using an array or singly-linked list associated with the currently rendering Fiber. A pure JS simulation of `useState` reveals how a pointer index and persistent state array track state across repeated render calls.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Maintain module-level `hooks = []` state storage array and `hookIndex = 0` pointer.
Define `useState(initialValue)`:
- Capture `currentIndex = hookIndex`.
- If `hooks[currentIndex] === undefined`, initialize `hooks[currentIndex] = (typeof initialValue === 'function' ? initialValue() : initialValue)`.
- Create setter: `setState = (newValue) => { hooks[currentIndex] = (typeof newValue === 'function' ? newValue(hooks[currentIndex]) : newValue); triggerRender(); }`.
- Increment `hookIndex++`.
- Return `[hooks[currentIndex], setState]`.
Before each render pass, reset `hookIndex = 0`.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: In real React (`packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberHooks.js`), each fiber has a `memoizedState` property pointing to the head of a linked list of Hook objects (`{ memoizedState, next, queue }`). Calling `useState` advances `workInProgressHook = workInProgressHook.next`.

complexity.space: O(H) heap memory where H is the number of hooks in the component.

edgeCasesHandled: Lazy initial state functions `useState(() => compute())` executed only on first mount.
Functional state updaters `setCount(prev => prev + 1)` receive the freshest state value.
Pointer reset guarantees identical hook matching across multiple renders.

specifications: Overreacted (Dan Abramov): How Does React Know Which Component Called A Hook?
verifiedRules: Hooks are tracked sequentially by invocation order on the fiber's memoizedState.
Resetting the cursor before each render is mandatory for hook synchronization.

questions.concept: Fiber memoizedState Linked List & Sequential Traversal
questions.problemStatement: Implement `createHookRunner()` that supports multiple calls to `useState()` across consecutive render passes, storing them in a linked-list structure and maintaining state continuity.
questions.interviewTrap: React does not use key names for hooks! It relies 100% on execution call order to pair each hook with its corresponding slot in the linked list.

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: Real React hooks are stored not in a flat array, but as a singly-linked list of Hook nodes on the Fiber: `fiber.memoizedState -> hook1 -> hook2 -> hook3 -> null`. Building a Multi-Hook Linked List Runner illustrates how `useState`, `useReducer`, and `useMemo` share the same linked list structure.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Define Hook node structure: `{ memoizedState, next }`.
During mount (`mountWorkInProgressHook`): instantiate a new Hook node, append to tail of linked list.
During update (`updateWorkInProgressHook`): advance `workInProgressHook = currentHook.next`, reading `memoizedState`.
Support multiple hook invocations per component in strict sequential order.
Component re-render traverses the existing linked list node-by-node.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: In `ReactFiberHooks.js`, `currentlyRenderingFiber` keeps track of the active fiber. Both `mount` and `update` phases execute different dispatchers: `HooksDispatcherOnMount` creates the nodes, while `HooksDispatcherOnUpdate` reads and updates existing nodes in the linked list.

complexity.time: O(1) access per hook call during render traversal.
complexity.space: O(H) nodes where H is count of hooks.

edgeCasesHandled: Multiple hooks of different types (state, memo, reducer) coexist on same linked list.
Preserves correct individual hook state across multiple re-render passes.
Reaching end of linked list properly matches expected hook count.

specifications: React Architecture Docs: Hooks Linked List Representation
verifiedRules: Fiber.memoizedState stores the head of the hook linked list.
Every hook node has a .next pointer pointing to the next hook.

questions.title: Rules of Hooks Dynamic Validator
questions.subtopicTitle: Hooks Linked List & Rules of Hooks
questions.concept: Detecting Conditional or Shuffled Hook Calls
questions.problemStatement: Implement `validateHookSequence(mountHooks, updateHooks)` that compares the sequence of hook types called on mount vs update. If update calls fewer hooks, more hooks, or a different hook type at any index, throws an Error detailing the exact violation.
questions.interviewTrap: This is the exact runtime error React throws: 'Rendered fewer hooks than expected. This may be caused by an accidental early return statement.'

testCases.name: Validates identical hook sequences across renders
testCases.testFn: return validateHookSequence(['useState', 'useEffect'], ['useState', 'useEffect']).valid;

testCases.name: Throws error when hook type order is transposed
testCases.input: swapped hooks throws type mismatch error

details.input: swapped hooks throws type mismatch error

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: The fundamental Rule of Hooks ('Only Call Hooks at the Top Level — do not call inside loops, conditions, or nested functions') exists because React relies exclusively on the sequential call order of hooks to match state. A dynamic validator detects hook count or type mismatches across renders and throws an error.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Maintain record of hooks called during initial mount: `expectedHookSequence = ['state', 'effect', 'state']`.
On subsequent re-renders, track each hook call index and type.
If a conditional statement omits a hook or changes the order (e.g. calling 'effect' when 'state' was expected):
Immediately detect mismatch: `Rendered fewer hooks than expected` or `Hook type mismatch at index i`.
Throw descriptive error matching React's internal invariant violation.
Validator confirms strict obedience to the Rules of Hooks.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: In React's `ReactFiberHooks.js`, if `updateWorkInProgressHook` finds that `nextHook` is null while the component is still executing hooks, React throws: `Error: Rendered more hooks than during the previous render`. If the component finishes with unvisited hooks left over, it throws: `Error: Rendered fewer hooks than during the previous render`.

complexity.time: O(H) validation over H hook calls.

edgeCasesHandled: Detecting conditionally omitted hooks.
Detecting hook type order swaps across renders.
Successful validation when hook sequences match identically.

specifications: React Official Docs: Rules of Hooks
verifiedRules: Hooks must be called in the exact same order on every render.
Violating call order corrupts internal linked list pointers and throws invariant errors.

subtopics.title: Stale Closures & Functional State Updates
subtopics.summary: Stale state in asynchronous callbacks, functional state updates, and useEvent RFC pattern.
subtopics.mentalModel: Callbacks defined inside component bodies capture state variables as they existed during that specific render. If the callback runs later asynchronously without reading a ref or using functional update `prev => ...`, it reads stale snapshot values.
subtopics.traps: Passing stale state to web socket listeners or intervals, causing updates to revert previous changes.

questions.title: Async State Updater Guard
questions.concept: Avoiding Stale Snapshots in Asynchronous Callbacks
questions.problemStatement: Implement `createSafeAsyncAccumulator(initialVal)` that provides `addAsync(amount)`: it simulates an asynchronous API delay, then safely adds `amount` to the current state using a functional updater pattern.
questions.interviewTrap: Reading `state + amount` after the await delay will drop any concurrent updates that finished while the promise was pending.

testCases.name: Safely aggregates concurrent async updates without losing data
testCases.testFn: const acc = createSafeAsyncAccumulator(0); await Promise.all([acc.addAsync(10, 20), acc.addAsync(20, 10)]); return acc.getState();

testCases.name: Maintains initial value
testCases.testFn: const acc = createSafeAsyncAccumulator(100); return acc.getState();

testCases.name: Handles sequential updates
testCases.testFn: const acc = createSafeAsyncAccumulator(0); await acc.addAsync(5, 5); await acc.addAsync(10, 5); return acc.getState();

details.name: Safely aggregates concurrent async updates without losing data
Maintains initial value
Handles sequential updates

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: A Stale Closure occurs when a function or asynchronous callback captures a variable from an older render pass's lexical scope. If state changes, the older callback still references the stale value. An Async State Updater Guard ensures state updates are dispatched safely using functional updaters.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Demonstrate stale closure problem: `setTimeout(() => setCount(count + 1), 1000)` captures `count = 0` at timer creation time; three concurrent clicks resolve to `1` instead of `3`.
Implement guard using functional state updater: `setCount(prev => prev + 1)`.
Functional updaters bypass the closed-over outer variable and read directly from React's internal pending update queue (`updateQueue`), guaranteeing monotonic accumulator increments.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: In `ReactFiberHooks.js`, updates are pushed onto a circular linked list `queue.pending`. When evaluated during the update phase, React loops through all pending update actions sequentially: `newState = action(currentState)`. Passing a function evaluates against the latest reduced accumulator value, completely circumventing closure capture.
edgeCasesHandled: Multiple rapid asynchronous updates (e.g. 5 concurrent delayed updates) correctly produce 5.
Sequential and interleaved updates preserve accurate running totals.
Eliminates race conditions between asynchronous network responses and current state.

specifications: React Official Docs: Queueing a Series of State Updates
Overreacted (Dan Abramov): A Complete Guide to useEffect (Stale closures section)
verifiedRules: Functional updates read from the reducer queue, not the component closure.
Direct state value references in async callbacks are inherently vulnerable to stale closures.

questions.title: Implement useInterval (Dan Abramov Pattern)
questions.concept: Mutable Saved Callback Ref to Eliminate Interval Teardowns
questions.problemStatement: Implement `createUseIntervalManager()` that accepts an interval callback and delay. Whenever the callback changes, update the internal saved reference WITHOUT restarting the interval timer.
questions.interviewTrap: Setting `callback` in the `useEffect` dependency array restarts the interval on every render, resetting the timer tick.

testCases.name: Invokes the freshest callback without restarting the timer
testCases.testFn: const manager = createUseIntervalManager(); let calledWith = ''; manager.setCallback(() => { calledWith = 'old'; }); manager.start(20); manager.setCallback(() => { calledWith = 'fresh-callback'; }); await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 35)); manager.stop(); return calledWith;

testCases.name: stop() halts timer ticks cleanly
testCases.testFn: const manager = createUseIntervalManager(); let count = 0; manager.setCallback(() => count++); manager.start(15); await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 25)); manager.stop(); await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 30)); return count;

testCases.name: Does not start timer if delay is null
testCases.testFn: const manager = createUseIntervalManager(); let count = 0; manager.setCallback(() => count++); manager.start(null); await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 30)); return count;

details.name: Invokes the freshest callback without restarting the timer
stop() halts timer ticks cleanly
Does not start timer if delay is null

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: Standard `setInterval` does not play well with React because it captures closures from when the interval was established. Dan Abramov's canonical `useInterval` pattern solves this using a mutable ref (`savedCallback`) that is updated on every render, allowing the interval to invoke the freshest callback without resetting the timer.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Define `useInterval(callback, delay)`.
Create a mutable reference: `const savedCallback = useRef()`.
In `useEffect`, update the ref on every render: `savedCallback.current = callback`.
In a secondary `useEffect` dependent only on `[delay]`:
- If `delay !== null && delay !== undefined`:
Setup timer: `const id = setInterval(() => savedCallback.current(), delay)`.
Return cleanup function: `clearInterval(id)`.
Provide a `stop()` method to set delay to null or clear the interval.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: `useRef` returns a stable object `{ current: value }` whose reference identity never changes across renders. Mutating `ref.current` updates the value in-place without triggering re-renders and without changing the dependency array of the interval effect. The interval closure calls `savedCallback.current()`, reading the fresh function reference dynamically.
edgeCasesHandled: Dynamic callbacks with closed-over state always execute with latest state.
Changing `delay` dynamically adjusts interval timing cleanly.
Passing `delay: null` pauses the interval without unmounting.
Calling `stop()` halts interval ticks immediately.

specifications: Dan Abramov: Making setInterval Declarative with React Hooks (Overreacted.io)
React Official Docs: Referencing Values with Refs
verifiedRules: Refs provide a mutable escape hatch across renders without re-triggering effects.
Separating callback storage from timer lifecycle prevents timer reset thrashing.

questions.title: Implement 'useEffectEvent' / useEvent Polyfill
questions.concept: Stable Identity Event Function with Always-Fresh Lexical Scope
questions.problemStatement: Implement `useEffectEvent(handler)`: returns a function whose reference identity NEVER changes across renders, but when called, ALWAYS executes the latest `handler` passed on the most recent render.
questions.interviewTrap: Developers often wrap handlers in `useCallback(fn, [deps])`, causing child components or effects to re-run whenever dependencies change. `useEffectEvent` extracts non-reactive event logic cleanly.

testCases.testFn: const manager = createEffectEventManager(); const fn1 = manager.stableEvent; manager.updateHandler(() => 1); const fn2 = manager.stableEvent; return fn1 === fn2;

testCases.name: Executes the newest handler reading fresh props
testCases.input: handler updated with new prop value
testCases.testFn: const manager = createEffectEventManager(); manager.updateHandler((msg) => `${msg}: light`); manager.updateHandler((msg) => `${msg}: dark`); return manager.stableEvent('Theme');

testCases.name: Passes all parameters and returns output correctly
testCases.testFn: const manager = createEffectEventManager(); manager.updateHandler((a, b) => a + b); return manager.stableEvent(10, 20);

Executes the newest handler reading fresh props
details.input: handler updated with new prop value

details.name: Passes all parameters and returns output correctly

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: React's proposed `useEffectEvent` (formerly `useEvent`) polyfill extracts non-reactive event logic out of effects. It returns a stable function reference that can read the latest props and state without needing to be listed in the effect's dependency array, preventing unnecessary effect re-executions.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Implement `useEffectEvent(callback)` (or `useEvent`):
Maintain a mutable ref holding the latest callback: `const callbackRef = useRef(callback)`.
Use `useInsertionEffect` (or synchronous layout assignment) to update `callbackRef.current = callback` before effects run.
Return a stable wrapped function `useCallback((...args) => callbackRef.current(...args), [])` with empty dependencies.
When invoked inside an effect, the wrapper calls the freshest `callbackRef.current` without forcing the effect to re-run when callback dependencies change.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: In React RFC for `useEffectEvent`, the returned function is tagged as an Event function. React forbids calling Event functions during the Render phase, restricting their execution to Effects and Event Handlers. It separates reactive values (which must trigger effects) from non-reactive logic (which needs current values on demand).

complexity.space: O(1) ref and memoized callback allocation.

edgeCasesHandled: Effect does not re-trigger when callback's captured state changes.
Callback always has access to the most recent state and props.
Throws or warns if invoked during render phase.

specifications: React RFC: useEffectEvent (Separating Events from Effects)
React Official Docs: Separating Events from Effects with useEffectEvent
verifiedRules: Effect Events are not reactive and must not be included in effect dependencies.
Effect Events must only be invoked from within effects or event handlers, never during render.

subtopics.title: useEffect vs useLayoutEffect vs useInsertionEffect
subtopics.summary: Paint blocking vs asynchronous passive effects, CSS-in-JS injection, and layout measurement.
subtopics.mentalModel: `useInsertionEffect` fires synchronously BEFORE DOM mutations (for CSS-in-JS injection). `useLayoutEffect` fires synchronously AFTER DOM mutations but BEFORE browser paint (for measurements). `useEffect` fires asynchronously AFTER the browser has painted pixels to screen.
subtopics.traps: Causing screen flickering by measuring DOM and setting state inside `useEffect` (requires `useLayoutEffect`).

questions.title: Effect Phase Order Logger
questions.problemStatement: Implement `logLifecyclePhases()` that returns an array with the exact execution order of: `'useInsertionEffect'`, `'DOM Mutation'`, `'useLayoutEffect'`, `'Browser Paint'`, and `'useEffect'`.
questions.interviewTrap: `useEffect` is passive and deferred until after paint. `useLayoutEffect` blocks painting.

testCases.name: Returns correct lifecycle sequence
testCases.testFn: return logLifecyclePhases();

testCases.name: useLayoutEffect runs before Browser Paint
testCases.testFn: const p = logLifecyclePhases(); return p.indexOf('useLayoutEffect') < p.indexOf('Browser Paint');

testCases.name: useEffect runs strictly after Browser Paint
testCases.testFn: const p = logLifecyclePhases(); return p.indexOf('useEffect') > p.indexOf('Browser Paint');

details.name: Returns correct lifecycle sequence
useLayoutEffect runs before Browser Paint
useEffect runs strictly after Browser Paint

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: React provides three distinct effect hooks that run at different stages of the commit phase: `useInsertionEffect` (runs first, synchronously before DOM mutations for CSS-in-JS libraries), `useLayoutEffect` (runs second, synchronously after DOM mutations before browser paint), and `useEffect` (runs third, asynchronously after browser paint).
stepByStepWalkthrough: Construct an Effect Phase Order Logger that executes simulated components.
Log each lifecycle step: Render -> Insertion Effects -> DOM Mutated -> Layout Effects -> Browser Paint -> Passive Effects.
Demonstrate that `useInsertionEffect` executes first, then `useLayoutEffect`, and finally `useEffect` asynchronously.
Verify cleanup execution order during unmounts and updates.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: In `ReactFiberCommitWork.js`, `commitMutationEffects` mutates the DOM. Immediately prior, `commitInsertionEffectOnFiber` fires `useInsertionEffect`. Immediately following, `commitLayoutEffects` fires `useLayoutEffect`. Then control yields to the browser paint engine. After paint, `flushPassiveEffects` drains `useEffect` queues.

complexity.time: O(E) where E is total count of effects across components.

edgeCasesHandled: Strict lifecycle sequence verification across all 3 hook types.
Effect cleanups run prior to re-execution in corresponding phases.
Passive effects defer execution until after paint.

specifications: React Official Docs: Synchronizing with Effects vs Layout Effects vs Insertion Effects
verifiedRules: useInsertionEffect runs synchronously before DOM mutations.
useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after DOM mutations and blocks paint.
useEffect runs asynchronously after browser paint.

questions.title: Simulate Synchronous Layout Measure Hook
questions.problemStatement: Implement `measureElementSynchronously(element, measureFn)` that executes `measureFn(element)` synchronously immediately after element attributes are written, guaranteeing that measurements occur before paint without flicker.
questions.interviewTrap: Measuring in `useEffect` causes a visible flicker: the user sees the unstyled/unmeasured element for one frame before it repositions.

testCases.name: Synchronously measures element geometry
testCases.testFn: const el = document.createElement('div'); return measureElementSynchronously(el, r => ({ width: r.width, height: r.height }));

testCases.name: Computes derived layout position immediately
testCases.testFn: const el = document.createElement('div'); return measureElementSynchronously(el, r => r.width / 2);

testCases.name: Returns synchronously without promises or timeouts
testCases.testFn: let measured = false; const el = document.createElement('div'); measureElementSynchronously(el, () => { measured = true; }); return measured;

details.name: Synchronously measures element geometry
Computes derived layout position immediately
Returns synchronously without promises or timeouts

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: `useLayoutEffect` is specifically designed for synchronous DOM layout measurements (e.g. `getBoundingClientRect()`, tooltip positioning, scroll offset adjustments) before the browser paints. Because it runs synchronously before paint, mutating the DOM inside `useLayoutEffect` prevents visible visual flicker.
stepByStepWalkthrough: Simulate synchronous layout measure hook `useLayoutMeasure(elementId)`.
Inside layout phase (synchronously after simulated DOM creation):
- Query DOM element: `document.getElementById(elementId)`.
- Read layout geometry: `rect = el.getBoundingClientRect()`.
- Compute derived positioning (e.g. tooltip coordinates: `top = rect.bottom + 8`).
- Return derived layout metrics synchronously without delays or promises.
Demonstrate that if this were done in `useEffect`, a frame would paint at old coordinates before jumping, causing a visible flicker.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: `useLayoutEffect` runs in the same synchronous turn as the commit phase. The browser's compositing and paint threads have not run yet. When `useLayoutEffect` updates state or modifies element styles, React performs an immediate synchronous sub-render before the browser renders pixels to the screen.

complexity.time: O(1) synchronous DOM query and calculation.

edgeCasesHandled: Returns synchronous layout position immediately without promises.
Calculates correct geometry based on element bounding rect.
Safely handles missing or unmounted elements.

specifications: React Official Docs: useLayoutEffect API reference
Kent C. Dodds: useEffect vs useLayoutEffect (Visual flicker analysis)
verifiedRules: useLayoutEffect blocks browser paint until execution finishes.
Synchronous DOM mutations in layout effects avoid visual glitches.

questions.title: Dual Queue Effect Scheduler (Layout Sync vs Passive Async)
questions.concept: Scheduler Separation of Layout and Passive Effect Queues
questions.problemStatement: Implement `createEffectScheduler()` that maintains two effect queues: `layoutQueue` (executed synchronously during commit) and `passiveQueue` (executed asynchronously after a tick). Returns an object with `scheduleLayout(fn)`, `schedulePassive(fn)`, `flushLayout()`, and `flushPassive()`.
questions.interviewTrap: If layout effects throw errors, the commit fails synchronously. If passive effects throw errors, they are surfaced in the next turn of the event loop.

testCases.name: Executes layout effects synchronously before passive effects

testCases.name: flushLayout clears all pending layout items
testCases.testFn: const s = createEffectScheduler(); s.scheduleLayout(() => 1); s.scheduleLayout(() => 2); return s.flushLayout();

testCases.name: flushPassive runs asynchronously after tick
testCases.input: passive flush resolves with executed values
testCases.testFn: const s = createEffectScheduler(); s.schedulePassive(() => 'async-done'); return await s.flushPassive();

flushLayout clears all pending layout items
flushPassive runs asynchronously after tick

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: A Dual Queue Effect Scheduler implements the two-tiered queuing architecture used by React: A Synchronous Layout Queue (processed immediately during commit) and an Asynchronous Passive Queue (processed in a microtask or message channel after paint).
stepByStepWalkthrough: Create `EffectScheduler` with `layoutQueue = []` and `passiveQueue = []`.
Method `scheduleLayout(effectFn)` pushes to `layoutQueue`.
Method `schedulePassive(effectFn)` pushes to `passiveQueue`.
Method `flushCommit()`:
- Synchronously drains and executes all effects in `layoutQueue`.
- Schedules asynchronous draining of `passiveQueue` via `setTimeout(flushPassive, 0)` or `postMessage`.
Provide `flushPassive()` to drain passive effects.
Verify that layout effects always execute before passive effects, even if scheduled in reverse order.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: In React source code (`packages/react-reconciler/src/ReactFiberWorkLoop.js`), `commitRoot` processes `commitLayoutEffects` directly. It then requests scheduling for `flushPassiveEffects` via `Scheduler_scheduleCallback(NormalSchedulerPriority, () => flushPassiveEffects())`.

complexity.time: O(L) synchronous layout flush + O(P) asynchronous passive flush.
complexity.space: O(L + P) queue storage for scheduled effect thunks.

edgeCasesHandled: Strict priority guarantee: all layout effects finish before any passive effect starts.
Clean draining: queues are emptied upon execution.
Asynchronous passive execution allows browser paint tick in between.

specifications: React Architecture: The Passive Effects Queue implementation
verifiedRules: Layout effects are flushed synchronously during the commit phase.
Passive effects are deferred to allow paint and prevent frame drops.
